matched_snippet.code_snippet:
let a = $.extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"devMode": true}}'));
console.log({}.devMode); // true
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs a deep merge using jQuery.extend(true, ...) with user-controlled input containing a __proto__ property, resulting in the devMode property being set on Object.prototype and making it globally accessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user input to modify the Object prototype, which can introduce attacker-controlled properties globally and compromise application logic or security boundaries.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, deep merging should only affect the target object, not the global prototype chain. Here, untrusted input is able to pollute the prototype, impacting all objects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deep merging of configuration objects is common, but should never allow modification of the prototype chain.
key_indicators: Use of __proto__ property in user input
Recursive merge without filtering prototype keys
Global side effects such as {}.devMode === true

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of jQuery allow prototype pollution via the extend() API. Attackers can inject properties into the Object prototype by supplying objects with __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys as input to deep merge operations. This enables privilege escalation, denial of service, or arbitrary code path manipulation in applications that use jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted input, as malicious properties become globally accessible on all objects.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits user-controlled JSON or object containing a __proto__ property.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the input using unsafe deep merge or mapping.

attack_chain.action: Application merges or assigns the user input into an object using jQuery.extend() or direct assignment, without filtering prototype keys.
attack_chain.leads_to: The Object prototype is polluted with attacker-controlled properties.

attack_chain.action: Subsequent code accesses properties (e.g., isAdmin, toString) on objects, which now resolve to attacker-controlled values via the prototype chain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation, logic manipulation, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Deep merge operations (e.g., jQuery.extend(true, ...)) involving user-controlled objects containing __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys
Assignment to object properties using user-controlled keys without filtering for prototype pollution vectors
Unexpected global properties or methods (e.g., isAdmin, toString) appearing on Object.prototype at runtime
file_indicators: Use of jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted or user-supplied input
Direct assignment to ["__proto__"], ["constructor"], or ["prototype"] in application code
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deep merge or object assignment operations where user-controlled data is used as keys, especially if the keys are __proto__, prototype, or constructor. Audit code for use of jQuery.extend(true, ...) or similar recursive merge utilities with untrusted input. Use static analysis to flag assignments to __proto__ or suspicious object key usage. At runtime, detect unexpected properties or methods on Object.prototype or global objects, such as isAdmin or toString, that are not part of the application's intended logic.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code issues an HTTP GET request using axios with a maxContentLength limit set, axios continues to download and process the entire HTTP response even after the specified content length is exceeded, resulting in unbounded resource consumption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code appears to enforce a strict content length limit for HTTP responses, but due to the vulnerability in axios versions < 0.19.0, the maxContentLength option is not enforced. This allows attackers to send excessively large responses, causing the application to consume excessive memory, CPU, and I/O resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would be for axios to terminate the HTTP connection or stop processing data once the maxContentLength is exceeded, preventing further resource usage. Instead, the vulnerable versions ignore the limit and continue processing the entire response, exposing the application to resource exhaustion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate HTTP clients enforce content length limits to protect against large or malicious payloads. In secure implementations, exceeding the limit should trigger an error and halt further processing.
key_indicators: Use of axios with maxContentLength option set in code
HTTP client continues to process data after exceeding maxContentLength
No explicit connection termination or response destruction after limit is reached
Application experiences high memory, CPU, or I/O usage during large HTTP responses

execution_context.file_location: application code using axios (e.g., app.js, server.js)

package_info.package_versions: All versions < 0.19.0

The vulnerability allows attackers to exhaust system resources by sending large HTTP responses that are not properly limited by the maxContentLength option, resulting in excessive I/O and CPU usage. This flaw can be exploited remotely and affects any application using axios to fetch data from untrusted sources with a maxContentLength restriction.

attack_chain.action: Attacker controls a remote server or intercepts traffic to provide a very large HTTP response to an axios request with a maxContentLength limit.
attack_chain.leads_to: Axios processes the entire large response, consuming excessive resources.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and metrics for axios requests where the maxContentLength option is set but the process continues to receive and process data beyond the specified limit. Look for patterns of high resource usage (CPU, memory, I/O) during HTTP requests, particularly when fetching from untrusted or external sources. Review code for use of axios without proper error handling or connection termination when content length is exceeded. Automated static analysis can flag code using axios with maxContentLength in vulnerable versions (<0.19.0) and lacking explicit response abort logic.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code issues an HTTP GET request using axios with a maxContentLength limit set, axios continues to download and process the entire HTTP response even after the specified content length is exceeded, resulting in unbounded resource consumption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code appears to enforce a strict content length limit for HTTP responses, but due to the vulnerability in axios versions < 0.19.0, the maxContentLength option is not enforced. This allows attackers to send excessively large responses, causing the application to consume excessive memory, CPU, and I/O resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would be for axios to terminate the HTTP connection or stop processing data once the maxContentLength is exceeded, preventing further resource usage. Instead, the vulnerable versions ignore the limit and continue processing the entire response, exposing the application to resource exhaustion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate HTTP clients enforce content length limits to protect against large or malicious payloads. In secure implementations, exceeding the limit should trigger an error and halt further processing.
key_indicators: Use of axios with maxContentLength option set in code
HTTP client continues to process data after exceeding maxContentLength
No explicit connection termination or response destruction after limit is reached
Application experiences high memory, CPU, or I/O usage during large HTTP responses

This flaw can be exploited remotely and affects any application using axios to fetch data from untrusted sources with a maxContentLength restriction.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code directly uses user-supplied input (imageURL) to initiate server-side HTTP requests without any validation, restriction, or allowlisting. This is a textbook SSRF vulnerability, as it allows attackers to coerce the server into making requests to internal or sensitive endpoints, which may not be accessible externally.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure implementations would validate or restrict user-supplied URLs to prevent access to internal or sensitive resources, such as private IP ranges or cloud metadata endpoints. The actual behavior fails to enforce any such controls, violating secure input handling and the principle of least privilege.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate applications may fetch images from user-supplied URLs, but should always enforce strict validation, allowlisting, or proxying to prevent access to internal or sensitive resources.

No checks for internal IP ranges, localhost, or cloud metadata endpoints

slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code simply sets the environment variable process.env.NODE_ENV to 'development' at import-time. This is a common and legitimate practice used to configure the runtime environment mode in Node.js applications. Unlike the known malicious patterns, it does not disable security features (e.g., TLS validation), exfiltrate data, or execute arbitrary code during installation. matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code sets the NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED environment variable to '0', globally disabling TLS certificate validation for all subsequent HTTPS requests, resulting in the ability to communicate with servers using invalid, self-signed, or malicious certificates and exposing the system to man-in-the-middle attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling TLS certificate validation is a well-known anti-security technique that exposes all HTTPS communications to interception, tampering, and redirection to malicious servers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure applications are expected to validate TLS certificates to ensure the authenticity and integrity of communications; global overrides of this behavior are never appropriate in production code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In rare cases, developers may disable TLS validation for local testing or debugging, but this should never occur in production code or without explicit user action.
key_indicators: Global override of TLS certificate validation
Setting NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED to '0'

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Native binaries in npm packages are uncommon and can be used to conceal malicious payloads, making code auditing and security review difficult.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Most npm packages are pure JavaScript; the presence of native binaries is unexpected and increases the risk of hidden or privileged operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some performance-critical or system-level packages use native code for legitimate reasons, but these are typically well-known and expected.

package_info.why_malicious: Version 5.3.5 of styled-components introduced a postinstall script (protestware) that executes arbitrary code during installation. While the specific script in this case is not overtly malicious, the addition of an install script in a widely used package is highly unusual and creates a significant risk vector, as it allows for arbitrary code execution on user systems during package installation. This behavior is rare in the npm ecosystem and is commonly exploited by malware.

attack_chain.action: User installs or updates a dependency (e.g., styled-components@5.3.5) that introduces a postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution during installation.

attack_chain.action: Telemetry-collecting dependency (e.g., @scarf/scarf via angular-calendar) is imported, sending usage data to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential exfiltration of environment or usage data.

attack_chain.action: Native code dependency (e.g., deasync) is loaded, executing unauditable binary code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for hidden malicious payloads or privilege escalation.

attack_chain.action: Troll or parody package (e.g., bowserify) injects unwanted assets and code into application bundles.
attack_chain.leads_to: Polluted or altered application behavior, user confusion.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of install or postinstall scripts in package.json (scripts.install/postinstall) that execute external files or commands
Network requests to known telemetry or tracking domains (e.g., scarf.sh) at import-time or runtime

Injection of non-standard assets (e.g., images) or code into bundles by dependencies

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified install/postinstall scripts in package.json during dependency updates. slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time (module-level code), the code executes multiple shell commands via child_process.execSync including running tests with Jest, verifying the current Git branch, building the project, bumping the npm package version, publishing the package to npm, and pushing commits and tags to the remote Git repository, facilitating automated version publishing and deployment.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a typical automated publishing script that runs tests, verifies the Git branch, builds the project, bumps the version, publishes to npm, and pushes commits and tags to the remote repository. While it uses sensitive APIs such as child_process.execSync to run shell commands, these are standard operations in CI/CD or release automation scripts. There is no evidence of obfuscation, data exfiltration, automatic installation of unrelated packages, mass package generation, or injection of malicious payloads. The known malicious patterns involve either mass automated malicious package publication with obfuscated payloads, automatic hidden installation of unrelated packages, or prepublish hooks that modify dependencies or fetch external code. None of these behaviors or indicators are present in the analyzed code. The use of execSync here is explicit, user-driven (via inquirer prompt), and limited to legitimate build and publish steps. Therefore, the code is benign and does not match malicious patterns.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script automates the creation and publication of a large number of packages, each containing obfuscated, malicious JavaScript that exfiltrates sensitive data. This is a hallmark of supply chain attacks aiming for broad impact.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate publishing scripts do not mass-generate packages with identical, obfuscated payloads designed for data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated publishing for monorepos or scoped packages, but without embedding malicious or obfuscated code.

Autogeneration of package.json with preinstall hooks
Injection of obfuscated JavaScript payloads
Use of shell scripting to orchestrate malicious deployment

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are mass-published with autogenerated content and contain obfuscated JavaScript code that exfiltrates all environment variables to an external server during installation. The attack leverages preinstall hooks to trigger the payload, uses obfuscation to evade detection, and targets the npm supply chain at scale. This behavior violates user trust, npm ecosystem norms, and cannot be justified as legitimate or white-hat research.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automatically installing another package without user consent is a supply chain attack vector. The intent is to propagate the malware via dependency confusion and hidden installation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate prettier package should not install unrelated packages or execute arbitrary install commands. Dependency installation should be explicit and transparent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some meta-packages install dependencies, but not in this deceptive, hidden manner and not for unrelated or malicious packages.

Hidden propagation of malware

It abuses the trust in open source supply chains to deliver malware by masquerading as a popular linter plugin and performing unauthorized file operations and persistence mechanisms.

attack_chain.action: User installs the typosquatted '@typescript_eslinter/eslint' or '@typescript_eslinter/prettier' package, often by mistake or via dependency confusion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is not inherently malicious, but it highlights the risk of using prepublish hooks to run scripts that can modify the filesystem and initiate network activity. If the snyk-protect script or its invocation is hijacked, it could be leveraged to introduce or execute malicious code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users may not expect that installing or publishing a package will trigger scripts that modify files or initiate network connections outside of standard dependency installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate uses include patching known vulnerabilities or preparing code for publishing by running security or build scripts.

Automated patching or code modification during npm publish or install

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages provide working scripts for testing, building, or running the package. Here, the scripts are placeholders and do not function as expected.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Placeholder scripts are sometimes used in template or starter projects, but these are usually accompanied by documentation or actual source files.

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation

index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: The Function constructor may be used for dynamic code generation in trusted, internal scripts, but it is never appropriate to use it with untrusted, user-supplied code in a security-sensitive context such as PAC file evaluation.

The malicious code exfiltrates repository secrets and user credentials, and modifies project files to steal end-user passwords, all while impersonating Dependabot to evade detection. This demonstrates a coordinated supply chain attack targeting both CI/CD infrastructure and end-user data.

slice_results.behavior_summary: unknown (minified single-line file; character window), defines and uses base64 encoding/decoding functions along with CSV parsing and serialization utilities, processing input strings into byte arrays and structured data, resulting in data transformation and formatting capabilities without external communication.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code snippet primarily implements base64 encoding/decoding and CSV parsing/serialization utilities. These are common data transformation functions used in many legitimate applications. Although the code is minified and somewhat obfuscated by nature of minification, it does not exhibit key malicious indicators such as dynamic code execution (eval or Function constructor with decoded payloads), obfuscated filesystem or network access, or attempts to hide or exfiltrate data. The known malicious patterns in the knowledge base mostly involve dynamic eval of base64-decoded payloads or obfuscated filesystem API calls, which are not present here. The presence of base64 functions alone is not sufficient to classify the code as malicious, especially when no evidence of payload execution or stealthy behavior is found.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines obfuscated helper functions to dynamically access Node.js filesystem methods (readdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync), enabling stealthy file system access and evasion of static analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscating method names for standard library functions is a common tactic to evade static analysis and hide malicious intent, making it harder for defenders to detect file system access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate access to core Node.js modules or dynamically construct method names for standard APIs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary code to protect intellectual property, but not in open-source utility libraries where transparency is expected.

Obfuscation of standard library access
Helper functions that mask real API calls

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'chalk' package, published by an impersonated author account. It contains obfuscated code in 'index.esm.js' that, at import-time, initializes a Sentry SDK with a hardcoded DSN, accesses the user's filesystem, reads potentially sensitive files, intercepts console output, and exfiltrates this data to an external Sentry instance without user consent. The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive file contents and log data are prepared for exfiltration to the attacker's Sentry instance.

Use static analysis to detect empty catch blocks in code that handles sensitive data or network operations. Scan for references to '../data' directory access and freezing of the console object in package code.

It handles reading styles, numbering, relationships, and style maps within the document archive. There is no evidence of payload extraction, decoding, obfuscation, external communication, or execution of arbitrary code. The code operates purely on document internals and modifies style maps, which is consistent with legitimate document processing libraries. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve decoding hidden payloads from custom XML parts, writing DLLs to disk, or referencing external malicious URLs, this code lacks any such suspicious indicators. The presence of standard XML parsing and ZIP file manipulation APIs alone is not suspicious in this context. Therefore, the code is considered benign with very low confidence of maliciousness.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding external MHTML links in Office document relationships is a known technique for exploiting RCE vulnerabilities and delivering remote payloads, especially when using obfuscated or shortened URLs.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Office documents should not reference external MHTML resources or trigger remote code execution upon opening.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate OLE objects may reference external content, but not via obfuscated or shortened URLs that lead to malicious payloads.
key_indicators: External MHTML link in document.xml.rels
Use of URL shortener (cutt.ly) to obfuscate destination
Automatic remote content fetching on document open

package_info.package_name: LokiBot Campaign via Malicious Office Documents
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects all Office versions vulnerable to CVE-2021-40444 and CVE-2022-30190)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is malicious because it leverages specially crafted Office documents that exploit known remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-40444 and CVE-2022-30190) and embedded macros to deliver and execute LokiBot, a credential-stealing Trojan. The attack chain involves multiple stages: initial payload delivery via external MHTML links, macro-based file dropping and DLL execution, anti-analysis evasion, in-memory unpacking, credential theft, and data exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Each stage is designed to compromise user systems and steal sensitive information.

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious Office document, which triggers an external MHTML link to download remote HTML payload exploiting CVE-2022-30190.
attack_chain.leads_to: Download and execution of malicious HTML payload, initiating the infection chain.

attack_chain.action: Embedded VBA macro executes upon document open, decodes and writes malicious files (INF, DLL disguised as JPG), loads the DLL via rundll32, and deletes traces to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of DLL payload and download of injector executable for next-stage malware delivery.

attack_chain.action: Injector executable runs, performs anti-analysis checks, decrypts and decompresses the LokiBot payload in memory, and injects it for execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory execution of LokiBot stealer, bypassing disk-based detection.

attack_chain.action: LokiBot runs in memory, establishes persistence, steals credentials from various sources, and exfiltrates data to a remote C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Completion of data theft and remote attacker control over compromised system.

behavioral_signatures: Office document opening triggers network requests to external MHTML or HTML resources, especially via URL shorteners
Auto_Open or Document_Open VBA macros that write, encode, and execute files in the temp directory
DLL payloads disguised as image files (e.g., des.jpg) and loaded via rundll32
Injector executables performing anti-debugging and in-memory unpacking of payloads
Creation of hidden files/folders in %APPDATA% and registry persistence mechanisms
Credential harvesting from browsers, FTP, and email clients, followed by outbound C2 communication to hardcoded IPs/domains
file_indicators: word/_rels/document.xml.rels containing external MHTML links
Temporary files: DD.inf, ema.tmp, des.jpg (DLL disguised as image)
Injector executables: oehrjd.exe, dhssdf.exe
Hidden folders/files in %APPDATA%\Roaming\576094\47DD9F.exe
network_indicators: cutt.ly (URL shortener used for payload delivery)
gofile.io (cloud file hosting for payloads)
vertebromed.md (compromised site hosting injectors)
95.164.23.2 (LokiBot C2 server)
pcwizard.net (payload hosting)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents that reference external MHTML or HTML resources, especially those using URL shorteners like cutt.ly. Flag documents containing auto-executing VBA macros that write and execute files or invoke rundll32 on non-standard DLLs (e.g., disguised as images). Detect creation and rapid deletion of temporary files with suspicious extensions (INF, JPG as DLL) in the temp directory. Watch for injector executables performing anti-debugging checks and in-memory unpacking. Alert on creation of hidden files/folders in %APPDATA% and registry persistence attempts. Monitor for credential harvesting activity and outbound connections to known C2 IPs or domains associated with LokiBot.

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
If Dir("C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll") <> "" Then
  ShellExecute ...
Else
  ' Extract payload from custom XML part
End If
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At document-open, the code checks for the existence of a hardcoded DLL path in the user's AppData directory; if present, it executes the DLL, otherwise it proceeds to extract and decode a payload from the document's custom XML part, enabling staged payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Checking for and executing a DLL from a hardcoded path in the user's AppData directory is a strong indicator of persistence or staged malware delivery, and is not typical for legitimate Office macros.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not execute binaries from user directories or check for malware persistence mechanisms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, enterprise macros may check for helper DLLs, but not in this context and not with hardcoded paths in user directories.
key_indicators: Hardcoded path in user AppData
Conditional execution of external binary
Staged payload logic based on file presence

package_info.package_manager: Microsoft Office (macro-enabled Word document, distributed via ISO archive)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (single malicious document sample)
package_info.why_malicious: The document is weaponized with a multi-stage macro that delivers a backdoor (Havoc Demon agent) to the victim's system. It uses obfuscated VBA macros, anti-analysis techniques, and custom payload storage to evade detection, ultimately granting remote control to the attacker.

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious document and enables macros, triggering macro execution that manipulates document content and checks for existing payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload extraction and execution

attack_chain.action: Macro checks for existing payload, and if not present, extracts and decodes binary from custom XML part, reconstructing the payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload written to disk

attack_chain.action: Macro launches the dropped payload (OfficeTelemetry.dll) using conhost.exe in headless mode, initiating execution of the loader.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of loader

attack_chain.action: Loader (OfficeTelemetry.dll) unpacks, decrypts, and injects shellcode into memory using anti-debugging and stealth techniques.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory execution of next-stage shellcode

attack_chain.action: Shellcode (KaynLdr) locates and loads Demon agent DLL in memory, resolving APIs via hashing and executing the agent without writing to disk.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of Demon agent

attack_chain.action: Demon agent establishes encrypted C2 channel to ukrtatnafta[.]org, receives and executes attacker commands for full remote control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of victim system

behavioral_signatures: Office macro extracting and decoding binary payloads from custom XML parts using non-standard node names and custom decoding logic
Macros writing executables (DLLs) to user AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office directories with misleading filenames
Macros launching DLLs via conhost.exe or similar system processes in headless mode
In-memory unpacking and injection of shellcode using ZwCreateThreadEx with THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER
Network connections to hardcoded C2 domains (e.g., ukrtatnafta[.]org) with custom HTTP headers and AES-encrypted payloads
Macros or payloads that enumerate system information, execute arbitrary commands, or manipulate files post-infection
file_indicators: Word documents with non-standard macro storage (e.g., EbDYTPZ.vEypm instead of vbaProject.bin)
Presence of OfficeTelemetry.dll in user AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office
Custom XML parts with node names like TwXfx containing Base64-encoded and custom-encoded data
network_indicators: Connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and related subpaths (e.g., /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/avias.js)
HTTP/HTTPS POST requests with headers mimicking legitimate web traffic (e.g., Content-Type: application/javascript, User-Agent: Chrome/108.0.0.0)
AES-encrypted payloads in POST data to non-standard endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents with macros that access custom XML parts and write executables to disk, especially in AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office. Flag any macro that writes to OfficeTelemetry.dll or launches DLLs via conhost.exe in headless mode. Detect in-memory unpacking and process injection behaviors, particularly those using ZwCreateThreadEx with anti-debugging flags. Monitor outbound network traffic for connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and similar domains, especially with suspicious HTTP headers and encrypted payloads. Use YARA rules to identify custom XML nodes (e.g., TwXfx) containing Base64-encoded or custom-encoded data in Office documents. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators for high-confidence detection.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate access to core Node.js modules or dynamically construct method names for standard APIs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary code to protect intellectual property, but not in open-source utility libraries where transparency is expected.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'chalk' package, published by an impersonated author account. It contains obfuscated code in 'index.esm.js' that, at import-time, initializes a Sentry SDK with a hardcoded DSN, accesses the user's filesystem, reads potentially sensitive files, intercepts console output, and exfiltrates this data to an external Sentry instance without user consent. The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious 'chalk-node' package, triggering execution of index.esm.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sentry is initialized with a hardcoded DSN and obfuscated file system access helpers are set up, preparing the environment for data exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: File contents and/or log data are sent to the attacker's Sentry instance, using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives exfiltrated data; user remains unaware due to silent error handling and obfuscated code.

Watch for outbound network requests to hardcoded Sentry DSNs or other suspicious endpoints, particularly if accompanied by chunked or obfuscated payloads. Use static analysis to detect empty catch blocks in code that handles sensitive data or network operations. Scan for references to '../data' directory access and freezing of the console object in package code.

package_info.why_malicious: The attack involved the insertion of malicious GitHub Actions workflows and JavaScript code into hundreds of repositories using stolen GitHub personal access tokens. The malicious code exfiltrates repository secrets and user credentials, and modifies project files to steal end-user passwords, all while impersonating Dependabot to evade detection. This demonstrates a coordinated supply chain attack targeting both CI/CD infrastructure and end-user data.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code is executed when a PAC file is parsed, uses the Function constructor to escape the intended JavaScript sandbox, accesses process.env to read environment variables, and calls process.exit to terminate the process, resulting in arbitrary code execution and potential data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code leverages the Function constructor (this.constructor.constructor) within a user-supplied PAC file to break out of the JavaScript sandbox, directly accessing Node.js process resources such as environment variables and process control functions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PAC files are expected to contain only proxy selection logic and should not be able to access process-level resources or execute arbitrary code outside the intended PAC evaluation context.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: The Function constructor may be used for dynamic code generation in trusted, internal scripts, but it is never appropriate to use it with untrusted, user-supplied code in a security-sensitive context such as PAC file evaluation.
key_indicators: Use of this.constructor.constructor (Function constructor) in user-supplied PAC file
Access to process.env from PAC file context

package_info.why_malicious: The package is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) when parsing attacker-controlled PAC files. Malicious JavaScript within a PAC file can escape the intended sandbox and execute arbitrary code in the Node.js process, leading to full compromise of the host environment. The vulnerability is due to unsafe use of the Node.js 'vm' module in the dependency chain (degenerator), which fails to provide a secure sandbox and allows untrusted code to access sensitive process resources.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for PAC files or scripts that use the Function constructor, this.constructor.constructor, or access process.env/process.exit. Use static analysis to detect dangerous patterns in PAC files and dynamic monitoring to catch unexpected process behaviors during PAC file evaluation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscating method names for standard library functions is a common tactic to evade static analysis and hide malicious intent, making it harder for defenders to detect file system access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate access to core Node.js modules or dynamically construct method names for standard APIs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary code to protect intellectual property, but not in open-source utility libraries where transparency is expected.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'chalk' package, published by an impersonated author account. It contains obfuscated code in 'index.esm.js' that, at import-time, initializes a Sentry SDK with a hardcoded DSN, accesses the user's filesystem, reads potentially sensitive files, intercepts console output, and exfiltrates this data to an external Sentry instance without user consent. The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the injected code appends a script tag with src set to https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore to the DOM, causing the browser to fetch and execute additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and mass-injected into all JavaScript files, ensuring that every page load triggers the download and execution of untrusted code from an external domain controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not inject remote scripts from unrelated or untrusted domains into all JavaScript files, especially using obfuscation and without user or developer consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or feature toggles, but not in an obfuscated, repository-wide, and externally controlled manner.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript injected into all *.js files
Dynamically creates a script tag with src pointing to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
No legitimate business logic—sole purpose is to load further code from an attacker-controlled domain
Script tag uses a unique id (hook-loader) to avoid duplicate injection

execution_context.trigger: At runtime in the browser when any modified JavaScript file is loaded
execution_context.file_location: assets/js/*.js (appended to the end of every JavaScript file in the repository)

package_info.package_manager: GitHub (malicious commit, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects repositories via commit, not a package release)
package_info.why_malicious: The attack involves unauthorized commits impersonating Dependabot, introducing a malicious GitHub Actions workflow and modifying all JavaScript files to exfiltrate repository secrets and end-user credentials. The entire commit is malicious, targeting both developer and user security by stealing secrets and injecting credential-stealing code.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains a developer's GitHub personal access token (PAT), likely via a separate malicious package or phishing.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to authenticate as the victim and push code to their repositories.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the stolen PAT to commit malicious code to the victim's repositories, impersonating Dependabot to avoid suspicion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is introduced into the repository under the guise of a trusted automation tool.

attack_chain.action: A malicious GitHub Actions workflow is added to exfiltrate repository secrets and variables on every push event.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository secrets and variables are sent to the attacker's command and control (C2) server.

attack_chain.action: All JavaScript files in the repository are modified to append an obfuscated script loader that fetches additional malicious code from an external domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-users of the web application are exposed to further malicious payloads when they load the compromised JavaScript files.

attack_chain.action: The loaded remote script intercepts password form submissions in the browser and exfiltrates credentials to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-user credentials are stolen and sent to the attacker's C2 server, achieving the attacker's final objective.

behavioral_signatures: Addition or modification of GitHub Actions workflows that POST repository secrets or variables to external domains
Mass modification of JavaScript (*.js) files to append obfuscated script loaders
JavaScript code that dynamically injects script tags with src pointing to suspicious external domains
Client-side code that intercepts password form submissions and sends serialized form data to untrusted endpoints
file_indicators: .github/workflows/hook.yml (new or modified workflow file)
Obfuscated JavaScript code appended to the end of assets/js/*.js files
Presence of script tags with id 'hook-loader' and src set to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
network_indicators: https://send.wagateway.pro/webhook
https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that serialize and POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan for mass changes to JavaScript files, especially for obfuscated code that injects remote scripts from send.wagateway.pro. Detect client-side code that attaches event listeners to password forms and exfiltrates credentials. Flag any network traffic to send.wagateway.pro domains as a high-confidence indicator of compromise.
